noticias.titulo: Quería quitar las aplicaciones que Android no me deja borrar. Así que le pedí a la IA mi propio desinstalador: en media hora lo tenía
noticias.resumen: Cada vez que compro un móvil, o analizo uno, este viene con un buen montón de aplicaciones que no necesito . La primera configuración suele ser larga, porque me dedico a iniciar sesiones, ordenar los escritorios y siempre quito app por app las que no necesito. El problema es que hay unas cuantas que no se dejan ni eliminar ni deshabilitar. Son las aplicaciones de sistema. Android facilita la personalización en mayor medida que iOS . Esta brecha se ha ido reduciendo con el paso del tiempo, siempre hasta cierto punto, porque Google continúa permitiendo el acceso al sistema con cierta…
noticias.contenido: Cada vez que compro un móvil, o analizo uno, este viene con un buen montón de aplicaciones que no necesito . La primera configuración suele ser larga, porque me dedico a iniciar sesiones, ordenar los escritorios y siempre quito app por app las que no necesito. El problema es que hay unas cuantas que no se dejan ni eliminar ni deshabilitar. Son las aplicaciones de sistema. Android facilita la personalización en mayor medida que iOS . Esta brecha se ha ido reduciendo con el paso del tiempo, siempre hasta cierto punto, porque Google continúa permitiendo el acceso al sistema con cierta profundidad. Si en mis tiempos jóvenes usaba Titanium Backup para una limpieza completa con root , ahora me conformo con ADB . Una app que programé con IA me ayuda en la tarea. Deshabilitando las apps de sistema en Android Desinstalación de apps de sistema con Brisa Desde el gestor de aplicaciones resulta posible eliminar las aplicaciones del usuario y también algunas de sistema. Aparte, varias aplicaciones más también pueden deshabilitarse: no se desinstalan físicamente, pero sí dejan de funcionar en segundo plano. Hay otras que no se dejan quitar de ninguna de estas dos formas. En Xataka Las mejores webs para bajar aplicaciones gratis y otro software de forma segura Dado que hace años que dejé de rootear mis móviles Android, siempre que quiero limpiar de manera profunda un teléfono acudía a Universal Android Debloater . Es una herramienta para PC que permite eliminar la instalación de casi cualquier app del teléfono, una acción que el gestor propio del teléfono no siempre permite. El Debloater usa ADB y sus comandos para obrar la magia, pero me hacía falta un PC. Prompt para Grok con el que empezó a crear la app Brisa Un día pensé: ¿por qué no tener en el móvil un desinstalador universal que funcionase internamente con ADB para así prescindir del ordenador ? Me serviría para aquellas aplicaciones tozudas que no se dejan ni eliminar ni deshabilitar desde el teléfono. Y, como Shizuku ya gestiona por sí sola las peticiones ADB desde el propio teléfono, solo necesitaba unir mi app a dicho Shizuku para obtener un desinstalador universal. Aproveché el acceso avanzado que ofrece Shizuku para tener una app de desinstalación más profunda que el gestor del sistema Para la tarea usé Grok en modo Build. Le pedí que quería una aplicación tipo Universal Debloater, con acceso a ADB a través de Shizuku. Le especifiqué que debía crear el APK y, tras unas cuantas iteraciones, y algo más de media hora de trabajo, me entregó una versión suficientemente estable. Grok la llamó Brisa , le dejé ese nombre. Un desinstalador local y en bloque Izquierda, desinstalación en bloque; derecha, proceso de desinstalación en segundo plano Android ya deja eliminar buena parte de las apps, aunque algunas de sistema se resisten. ADB puede meter mano casi hasta la cocina, siempre con cuidado: hay cierto riesgo de fastidiar el sistema si se toca según qué tecla. Brisa facilita el trabajo, incluye una papelera, restauración y un detalle que me parece importante: puede encadenar la desinstalación de múltiples aplicaciones . No solo de sistema. Con la app que me hizo Grok puedo marcar lo que no quiero de una lista, tanto da que sea de sistema como de usuario. Tras el enlazado con Shizuku (esta se aprovecha de ADB inalámbrico ), Brisa realiza un proceso automático para el que antes yo necesitaba un buen rato de dedicación. Y puede sacar de mi móvil el rastro de aplicaciones que desde Android no se dejan ni deshabilitar. DroidDeck convierte tu móvil Android en una Steam Deck para jugar a juegos de PC en local y sin streaming: así funciona Aparte de quitar el bloatware , Brisa hace rápida la eliminación y mucho más sencilla. Puede rescatar las aplicaciones eliminadas y las deshabilitadas. Todo con una interfaz amigable y fácil de utilizar. Y como sé de qué manera está hecha, y me impliqué en todo el proceso, me aseguro la privacidad de todos los datos. Cómo probar Brisa Lo ideal es que te armes tú la app de desinstalación a tu manera. Si quieres probar la mía, la he dejado en este enlace . Necesitas Shizuku instalado en tu Android y activo: en Android 11 o superior basta con la depuración inalámbrica, sin cables ni ordenador. Como dije antes, eliminar algunas aplicaciones es un riesgo: ve con mucho cuidado. Todos los cambios que hagas pueden deshacerse, pero si el sistema da error porque le falte algo es probable que ya no puedas arrancar correctamente el teléfono. Imagen de portada | Iván Linares editada - La noticia Quería quitar las aplicaciones que Android no me deja borrar. Así que le pedí a la IA mi propio desinstalador: en media hora lo tenía fue publicada originalmente en Xataka por Iván Linares .

noticias.titulo: Residents raise $30,000 to bring first grocery store to Alabama neighbourhood in 70 years
noticias.resumen: After nearly 70 years without a grocery store, Birmingham's Fountain Heights neighbourhood has opened the We All Eat Market. Developed by a local farming cooperative, the $1 million project received $30,000 in grassroots contributions and $150,000 from the city. The market will sell locally grown food, support small farmers and offer discounts to eligible customers.

Norway’s largest Viking hoard yields rare King Olaf coin not found in country since 1924
noticias.resumen: A rare coin minted during King Olaf Haraldsson's reign around 1025 has been identified in Norway's Morstad Viking hoard. It is only the second coin of this type found in Norway, the previous one dating back to 1924. The coin also offers clues about the king's use of Christian symbols and its circulation in commercial transactions.

The findings suggest that the tears formed through distinct geodynamic mechanisms and may have influenced regional tectonic deformation and magmatic activity.

noticias.titulo: MAX POWER: NASA’s Inaugural Aerospace Expo Ignites America’s Future
noticias.resumen: Thousands gathered over several days in early November to experience MAX POWER – NASA’s first exhibition of America’s superiority in space, aeronautics, and technology on and around the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The multi-day, family-friendly event honored the nation’s 250th anniversary and served as a culmination of the agency’s Inspiration Tour. Among the […]
noticias.contenido: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman skydives into the agency’s MAX POWER expo and air show on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The agency’s inaugural MAX POWER is an aerospace festival celebrating the past, present, and future of flight and space exploration in honor of America’s 250th anniversary. Credit: NASA/Jonathan Shaban Thousands gathered over several days in early November to experience MAX POWER – NASA’s first exhibition of America’s superiority in space, aeronautics, and technology on and around the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The multi-day, family-friendly event honored the nation’s 250th anniversary and served as a culmination of the agency’s Inspiration Tour . Among the many highlights, NASA welcomed President Donald J. Trump to MAX POWER, which featured flyovers and a skydive from NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and announced a new X-plane, astronaut candidate recruitment, a student Moon Base challenge, and discussed the agency’s latest lunar exploration plans. “It was a great week at NASA Kennedy, where we were joined by the President and federal, state, international, and industry leaders,” said Isaacman. “During our nation’s 250th birthday, the year of Artemis II’s voyage around the Moon, we were thrilled to invite the public out to see the rockets, the landers, the rovers, and the technology that will return astronauts to the lunar surface and build the base, not to mention witness a wonderful airshow that included NASA research aircraft and was headlined by the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds.” Through multiple park experiences, NASA and external collaborators at UP.Summit, Air Dot Show, Purpose Entertainment, and Delaware North each hosted a variety of private and public events Nov. 4-8. Teams showcased the newest aircraft, rovers, autonomous vehicles, and technologies defining the future of air and space. Astronauts, scientists, engineers, pilots, and subject matter experts were on hand for a variety of moderated discussions, appearances, and more. Some of the key announcements made at MAX POWER included: NASA opened astronaut applications through Thursday, Dec. 3, seeking future explorers to fly Artemis and low Earth orbit missions, and help build humanity’s first lunar outpost. NASA also challenged students to a $1 million competition to design innovative solutions for the Moon Base, giving participants an opportunity to develop necessary skills for careers in the space industry while helping advance new concepts for Moon Base technologies. Agency leadership announced numerous awards, task orders, and selections involving 12 companies to advance development of the Moon Base , marking significant progress toward establishing humanity’s first permanent presence on the lunar surface. The announcements spanned transportation, technology, and science initiatives, including moving forward with development of PROMISE, NASA’s nuclear-powered lunar rover. Isaacman unveiled the agency’s newest X-plane, the X-70 Fractal , an experimental aircraft which could revolutionize crewed flight with its maneuverability and flight-control technology. While guests journeyed between three park locations on the ground at NASA Kennedy’s historic Shuttle Landing Facility, T-38s, F-5s, and an ER-2 sped overhead during four flyovers, several of which were piloted by Isaacman. Some guests also were invited to a black-tie gala featuring agency leadership remarks and panel discussions with Apollo and Artemis astronauts. NASA’s Artemis III crew members also took to the stage during the astronaut announcement, previewing their test flight in low Earth orbit in 2027. NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, and Andre Douglas, as well as ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano all will fly aboard Orion, will launch on the SLS (Space Launch System), to test docking and rendezvous capabilities with the Blue Origin Blue Moon lander and SpaceX Starship lunar lander test articles, respectively, laying the groundwork to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028. Finally, while this expo was the first for NASA, there is much more to come. As part of a public/private partnership, NASA and its partners also announced CAPEWEEK: The Great American Aerospace and Technology Expo at Kennedy. The new annual expo will debut March 27 through April 2, 2028, at Kennedy’s Shuttle Landing Facility, with a footprint expected to ultimately grow upward of 500,000 people. “It was an educational and inspirational event, with a student Moon Base science challenge, a call for more NASA astronauts, and the unveiling of a new X-plane,” said Isaacman. “All credit goes to the NASA workforce and our partners, doing the work each day to bring the NASA missions to reality, and events like this so successful. So much so that we are doing it again, only bigger. CAPEWEEK begins in 2028.” To learn more about NASA’s missions, visit: https://www.nasa.gov Pilots perform flight maneuvers for NASA’s MAX POWER expo and air show on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Bresnik, along with NASA astronaut Frank Rubio, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, and Artemis III backup crew member Bob Hines each rode through the park in a vintage Corvette Credit: NASA/Clayton Rougelot NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman skydives into the agency’s MAX POWER expo and air show on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Credit: NASA/Amber Jean Notvest On Nov. 6, 2026, Purpose Entertainment hosted the Artemis Celebration Gala at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Merritt Island, Florida. Held on the eve of NASA’s MAX POWER event, the gala celebrated the explorers, innovators, and visionaries advancing the next era of human spaceflight. The event honored the successful completion of the agency’s Artemis II mission, marking a historic milestone in America’s return to deep space exploration. As one of the signature events concluding the nation’s 250th anniversary celebration, the gala commemorated the achievements of Artemis II while looking ahead to humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the Artemis campaign. noticias.titulo: NASA’s ESCAPADE Completes Powered Earth Flybys, Now En Route to Mars
noticias.resumen: NASA’s two ESCAPADE (Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers) spacecraft have each successfully completed a powered Earth flyby, using Earth’s gravity in combination with a sustained engine burn to slingshot themselves toward Mars. With these successful maneuvers complete, the twin spacecraft are on target to reach the Red Planet in September 2027. “This is […]
noticias.contenido: NASA’s two ESCAPADE (Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers) spacecraft have each successfully completed a powered Earth flyby, using Earth’s gravity in combination with a sustained engine burn to slingshot themselves toward Mars. With these successful maneuvers complete, the twin spacecraft are on target to reach the Red Planet in September 2027. “This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we’ve now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days,” said Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for the Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In November 2026, each of NASA’s two ESCAPADE (Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers) spacecraft executed a powered flyby of Earth, combining Earth’s gravity with an engine burn, to slingshot itself toward Mars. The first spacecraft made its closest approach around 5 a.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 7, and the second did so two days later, around 6 a.m. EST on Monday, Nov. 9. In this animation, each spacecraft’s approximately 9-minute trans-Mars injection burn appears as an orange arc along the spacecraft’s trajectory. Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger The two ESCAPADE spacecraft launched from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on Nov. 13, 2025, when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun. So instead of heading straight for the Red Planet, as most other Mars missions have done, both spacecraft entered a “loiter” or “Earth-proximity” orbit. They charted a first-of-its-kind, kidney-bean-shaped course around a place in space about a million miles from Earth called Lagrange point 2, which is a gravitational balancing point on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun. Then they headed back toward Earth to perform this gravitational slingshot maneuver around our planet once Earth and Mars were favorably aligned. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The ESCAPADE mission is pioneering a unique path to get to Mars. After launch in November 2025, the two ESCAPADE spacecraft looped around the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 (L2), in an “Earth-proximity” or “loiter” orbit that allowed the spacecraft to return to Earth in November 2026 and use our planet’s gravity to slingshot themselves to Mars. Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger “With this loiter orbit and Earth flyby, ESCAPADE is pioneering a new strategy for getting to Mars,” said Jeff Parker of Advanced Space, lead mission designer. “This method provides the flexibility to launch almost anytime and then use Earth’s gravity to get a boost to Mars, rather than waiting every two years to launch there directly when the planets are aligned.” The first ESCAPADE spacecraft completed its close approach to Earth and its approximately 9-minute trans-Mars injection burn — the engine firing that commits the spacecraft to its path to Mars — at 5 a.m. EST on Nov. 7, when it was about 1,000 miles above the planet’s surface. The second spacecraft followed suit two days later, completing its close approach and engine burn at 6 a.m. EST on Nov. 9, when it was about 650 miles above the planet’s surface. In the mission operations center at the University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory (SSL), Robert Lillis, ESCAPADE’s principal investigator (bottom right), awaits a signal after the first spacecraft performed an engine burn that initiated a powered Earth gravity assist on Nov. 7, 2026. Also pictured in the foreground (from left to right) are SSL aerospace engineer Sasha Courtade, SSL mission operations manager Mark Lewis, and SSL mission operations engineer Brett Bonelli. Alan Toth/UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory These powered flybys of Earth set both spacecraft on course for their 10-month cruise to Mars, culminating with their Mars orbit insertion burns planned for Sept. 7 and Sept. 9, 2027. Once in orbit around Mars, the two spacecraft will fly in formation to study how a million-mile-per-hour stream of material flowing from the Sun, known as the solar wind, interacts with the Martian environment and how that drives atmospheric loss at Mars. “By better understanding how the solar wind affects the Martian environment, ESCAPADE’s findings could help us plan and prepare for future human exploration of the Red Planet,” said Michele Cash, ESCAPADE program scientist at NASA Headquarters. The twin ESCAPADE spacecraft have already taken some science observations during their loiter orbit as they flew multiple times through Earth’s magnetotail, a part of our planet’s magnetic environment that gets stretched away from Earth, opposite the Sun, by the solar wind. During the 10-month trip to Mars, the spacecraft also will be able to study the dynamics of the solar wind between Earth and Mars. Along the way, the spacecraft will perform a series of trajectory correction maneuvers to adjust their path and ensure they are on a precise course to rendezvous with Mars in September 2027. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video With ESCAPADE’s trans-Mars injection burns complete, the two spacecraft (represented by the central, teal arc) are traveling away from Earth (represented by the inner, blue orbit) and headed toward Mars (represented by the outer, red orbit). Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger When they reach Mars, two days apart, each spacecraft will fire its engine for about 11 minutes to slow down and enter orbit around the planet. The spacecraft then will take several months to maneuver into their first science formation, where they will follow one another in the same orbit to study how the planet’s environment changes with time and location. Science operations are expected to begin in June 2028. Six months later, the two spacecraft will shift into different orbits, with one traveling farther from Mars to observe the incoming solar wind and the other staying closer to the planet to study how Mars responds to the solar wind in real time. That science campaign is scheduled to last five months. “This will be the first science mission to choreograph two orbiters around Mars, and the first time we will be able to make coordinated observations of the Martian environment from two different locations simultaneously,” said ESCAPADE’s principal investigator, Rob Lillis of the University of California, Berkeley. Funded by NASA’s Heliophysics Division, ESCAPADE is part of the agency’s SIMPLEx (Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration) program, which supports missions that explore the solar system in innovative ways with smaller budgets. The University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory leads the mission with key partners Rocket Lab; NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University; Advanced Space; and Blue Origin. “The ESCAPADE mission continues the scientific legacy of historical Mars missions with a dedicated team driving new innovations for its journey to and at the Red Planet,” said Skyler Kleinschmidt, ESCAPADE program executive at NASA Headquarters. noticias.titulo: La Tierra tiene una invitada por Navidad: una miniluna de dos metros que vino en abril y se irá después de las fiestas
noticias.resumen: Estas Navidades, la Tierra tendrá una invitada muy especial. Una miniluna que vino a visitarnos el pasado mes de abril y que ha decidido quedarse hasta que pasen las fiestas. Obviamente, las rocas espaciales no deciden nada, permíteme la licencia literaria. Este objeto fue detectado orbitando a nuestro planeta en agosto de este año, aunque los cálculos de su trayectoria han demostrado que llevaba junto a nosotros cuatro meses. Estos mismos cálculos señalan que seguirá dando vueltas a nuestro alrededor más o menos hasta después de Navidad. Para principios de 2027 ya se habría marchado, aunque…
noticias.contenido: Estas Navidades, la Tierra tendrá una invitada muy especial. Una miniluna que vino a visitarnos el pasado mes de abril y que ha decidido quedarse hasta que pasen las fiestas. Obviamente, las rocas espaciales no deciden nada, permíteme la licencia literaria. Este objeto fue detectado orbitando a nuestro planeta en agosto de este año, aunque los cálculos de su trayectoria han demostrado que llevaba junto a nosotros cuatro meses. Estos mismos cálculos señalan que seguirá dando vueltas a nuestro alrededor más o menos hasta después de Navidad. Para principios de 2027 ya se habría marchado, aunque posiblemente vuelva a casa dentro de 10 años. Al final, las minilunas siempre nos acaban abandonando . Una atracción irresistible . Según los cálculos realizados por los científicos, 2026 QQ8 tarda unos 359 días en dar la vuelta al Sol, casi lo mismo que la Tierra. Se acerca a nosotros más o menos cada diez años, por lo que no es su primera visita. Sin embargo, esta vez se acercó tanto y a una velocidad relativa tan baja que la atracción gravitatoria de la Tierra lo capturó y lo introdujo en una órbita a su alrededor. Así, quedó convertido en una miniluna, aunque no estará ahí para siempre. Lunas que vienen y van . El anuncio sobre este objeto, llamado 2026 QQ8, se hizo el 29 de octubre. Lo ha comunicado el Minor Planet Center , una institución que se encarga de estudiar los cometas, asteroides y otros objetos menores del Sistema Solar. También estudia las minilunas, pequeños objetos que orbitan temporalmente en torno a la Tierra, pero sin llegar a ser satélites fijos. Son tan comunes que, según un estudio reciente , nuestro planeta podría tener normalmente hasta seis minilunas girando a su alrededor. Algunas son fragmentos de nuestro propio satélite, aunque también hay otros tipos de objetos. De media miden unos 75 centímetros y su estancia media es de aproximadamente 9 meses. En Xataka La Luna estaría compuesta por un fragmento de la Tierra y eso es un giro que nadie esperaba No hay nada que temer . Ya hemos visto que este objeto se ha convertido en satélite temporal porque se acercó mucho a nuestro planeta. Podríamos preguntar si dicho acercamiento supone un peligro. Sin embargo, hay varios motivos para estar tranquilos con respecto a eso. Para empezar, aunque 2026 QQ8 es un poco más grande que la media de minilunas, sigue siendo un objeto pequeño, de apenas 2 metros de diámetro. Si se acercase demasiado a la Tierra se quemaría casi por completo al cruzar la atmósfera y se convertiría en una bola de fuego. No caerían restos peligrosos a la superficie. Además, no está tan cerca. Su punto más cercano a la Tierra está a 568.000 km, bastante más lejos que nuestra propia Luna. Hablando de la Luna… ¿por qué ella sí? Muchísimos objetos se convierten en minilunas temporales y luego siguen su camino. En cambio, la Luna se quedó unida a nuestro planeta para siempre. Hay varios argumentos que explican esto. En primer lugar, 2026 QQ8 y el resto de minilunas son objetos de paso. Circulan alrededor del Sol, no de la Tierra, lo que pasa es que a veces se encuentran con nosotros y son atraídos temporalmente. La Luna, según la hipótesis más aceptada sobre su origen, se formó en la propia Tierra, a partir de los escombros derivados del impacto de un objeto del tamaño de Marte . Por otro lado, la Luna está mucho más cerca que esos objetos, aproximadamente a unos 384.000 kilómetros. Con todo esto, la interacción entre la Tierra y sus minilunas es mucho más débil que la de nuestro planeta con su satélite. Hay un último factor . Para quedarse con un objeto , un planeta tiene que quitarle energía orbital. En el Sistema Solar primitivo, el gas que rodeaba a los planetas jóvenes podía frenar objetos hasta capturarlos, pero hoy no existe un disco denso así alrededor de la Tierra. Por eso las minilunas pueden escapar con facilidad. La Luna, en cambio, no necesitó ser capturada, porque nació ya ligada a nuestro planeta. Esta se irá, como lo hacen todas, pero antes de eso se quedará una buena temporada de visita. Y posiblemente volverá dentro de una década. Al final, la Tierra siempre se convierte en un buen lugar al que volver. noticias.titulo: Watching others pays off: Attentive macaques benefit from observing their group mates interacting
noticias.resumen: Monkeys constantly observe and evaluate their social environment. It stands to reason that the social and mental abilities required to do so were favored by evolution. After all, these abilities should influence how an animal interacts with its conspecifics and, as a result, what social position it can attain within the group's hierarchy. Researchers from the DPZ and the University of Göttingen have now investigated whether this widely held assumption is correct by studying 46 wild male Assamese macaques in Thailand. The paper is published in the journal Current Biology.

noticias.titulo: Promising new biomarkers to diagnose feline chronic kidney disease
noticias.resumen: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is common in cats but often goes undiagnosed until it's at a late stage. Thanks to a recent study published in the Journal of Proteome Research, researchers have new leads to determine how feline CKD develops. The paper reports collections of potential protein biomarkers in urine that could help veterinarians detect different stages of the disease and develop more targeted and effective treatments for this irreversible ailment.

noticias.titulo: Las claves del escándalo que sacude al CEO de Nvidia: espionaje, infidelidad y la disputa entre China y EE.UU.
noticias.resumen: Pekín calificó de “calumnias” las versiones sobre una supuesta operación de inteligencia para acercarse a Jensen Huang; la empresa abrió una investigación independiente y Donald Trump defendió al empresario
noticias.contenido: TAIPÉI.– China rechazó este lunes las acusaciones de que sus servicios de inteligencia habrían organizado una operación para obtener información confidencial del director ejecutivo de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, mediante una empresaria con la que mantenía una relación sentimental , un romance con repercusiones internacionales. Pekín calificó las versiones como “infundadas” y una campaña de desprestigio, mientras que la compañía estadounidense abrió una investigación independiente para determinar si el ejecutivo pudo haber sido objeto de una operación de espionaje y si se comprometió información estratégica . El diario Global Times, un medio estatal chino, sostuvo que cada vez que las relaciones entre China y Estados Unidos comienzan a mejorar, “a menudo hay quienes disparan desde las sombras” , en una referencia a lo que presentó como un intento de perjudicar el vínculo bilateral. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson on the Chinese spy allegation against Nvidia’s Jensen Huang: The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China. pic.twitter.com/E4lPPngU6S — Clash Report (@clashreport) November 9, 2026 El caso combina una relación extramatrimonial, sospechas de inteligencia extranjera y una de las disputas tecnológicas más sensibles entre Estados Unidos y China : el acceso de Pekín a los chips avanzados necesarios para desarrollar inteligencia artificial. Huang, de 63 años, reconoció ante sus empleados que había sido infiel a su esposa y asumió la responsabilidad por sus actos, aunque no identificó a la mujer involucrada. La identidad de la empresaria señalada, sus vínculos con una compañía investigada por presunto contrabando de chips y las posibles implicancias para la seguridad nacional estadounidense están en el centro de la controversia. ¿Qué hizo Jensen Huang? El fundador y director ejecutivo de Nvidia admitió haber mantenido una relación íntima con una empresaria china identificada como Alice Huang , también conocida como Huang Le, que habría sido investigada por las autoridades estadounidenses por sus presuntos vínculos con los servicios de inteligencia de Pekín . Según reveló The New York Times , la inteligencia estadounidense concluyó que la mujer recopilaba información sobre Huang para transmitirla a China . El diario también informó que el empresario había desarrollado una relación estrecha con ella, aunque no precisó qué tipo de información habría podido obtener ni si llegó a compartir datos confidenciales. El domingo, Huang envió una carta a los empleados de Nvidia en la que reconoció la infidelidad y pidió disculpas a su familia, a sus colaboradores y a los integrantes de la junta directiva. “ Le fui infiel a mi esposa. Mis acciones la lastimaron a ella y a nuestros hijos. No hay excusa para lo que hice. Lo siento muchísimo”, escribió. También aseguró que asumía “toda la responsabilidad” por sus decisiones y pidió que se respetara la privacidad de su familia. En el mismo mensaje se refirió a las preocupaciones sobre seguridad nacional y confirmó que apoyaría plenamente la investigación independiente iniciada por la compañía. ¿Quién es Alice Huang? Los datos públicos sobre Alice Huang son escasos. Es ciudadana china, no tiene parentesco con el ejecutivo de Nvidia y habría ocupado un cargo jerárquico en Megaspeed International , una empresa de computación en la nube con sede en Singapur . Según información publicada por medios internacionales, habla inglés con fluidez y tiene contactos de alto nivel en el sector de los chips de inteligencia artificial . Un perfil localizado en una base de datos china de fondos de inversión indica que habría trabajado en el banco HSBC y como periodista en los medios estatales CCTV y Hunan TV . Sin embargo, la autenticidad de ese perfil no pudo ser verificada de manera independiente. Las versiones sobre la relación entre ambos también se apoyan en registros fotográficos y audiovisuales. Una imagen publicada en LinkedIn de una fiesta del sector tecnológico en 2024 parece mostrar a Huang sentado junto a una mujer identificada como Alice. En 2025, ambos asistieron a una cena organizada por el empresario en un restaurante de Taipéi, durante la feria tecnológica Computex. Las imágenes tomadas por periodistas muestran al ejecutivo con el brazo alrededor de la mujer, que lo besa en el cachete . Más tarde, los dos abandonaron el lugar en el mismo automóvil. Alice Huang was previously spotted gently stroking Jensen Huang’s back, kissing him on the cheek, and leaving together in the same car during a visit to Taipei. https://t.co/9vATCwFv4w pic.twitter.com/qfyaBJpgx9 — HouseOfVanity (@HouseOfVanity88) November 9, 2026 ¿Qué es Megaspeed y por qué está bajo sospecha? Megaspeed International es una compañía de centros de datos que alquila capacidad de procesamiento a otras empresas para entrenar y ejecutar sistemas de inteligencia artificial. Según su página web, es un socio comercial del negocio de computación en la nube de Nvidia en Asia-Pacífico y ofrece acceso a algunos de sus procesadores más avanzados. La empresa ya estaba bajo escrutinio de las autoridades estadounidenses por sospechas de que habría facilitado el acceso de China a chips de Nvidia cuya exportación está restringida por Washington. Según The New York Times , Estados Unidos investigaba desde 2024 el posible papel de Megaspeed en el traslado de procesadores avanzados hacia China . Singapur también habría abierto averiguaciones e interrogado a Alice Huang en 2025. En diciembre de 2025, la compañía rechazó informaciones sobre un presunto contrabando de chips y sostuvo que contenían “datos engañosos e insinuaciones incorrectas” . Bloomberg había informado previamente sobre una investigación en Singapur relacionada con esas sospechas. ¿Por qué el caso es grave para Estados Unidos? La controversia llega en un momento de máxima sensibilidad en la competencia tecnológica entre Washington y Pekín. Desde 2022, Estados Unidos impone restricciones a la exportación de los chips de inteligencia artificial más avanzados de Nvidia hacia China , con el argumento de que podrían utilizarse para desarrollar capacidades militares y tecnológicas estratégicas. Huang fue uno de los principales críticos de esas limitaciones. En los últimos años presionó al gobierno estadounidense para flexibilizar las restricciones y defendió la posibilidad de mantener el acceso de Nvidia al mercado chino. Sus gestiones tuvieron resultados durante la presidencia de Donald Trump. Este año consiguió autorización para vender a China los procesadores H200 , aunque no está claro si Pekín permitirá que sus empresas los compren en grandes cantidades. Antes también había impulsado la comercialización de los H20, modelos menos avanzados diseñados para el mercado chino y adaptados a las restricciones estadounidenses. La preocupación de Washington es que una eventual operación de inteligencia pudiera haber aprovechado los contactos personales del ejecutivo para acceder a información comercial, tecnológica o estratégica de una compañía central para la industria estadounidense. Por ahora, no hay pruebas públicas de que Huang haya entregado información confidencial ni de que conociera las supuestas actividades de espionaje de la empresaria. La controversia también llegó al Congreso estadounidense. Legisladores republicanos de alto rango solicitaron reuniones informativas con Huang para conocer los detalles de las acusaciones y sus posibles implicancias para la seguridad nacional. ¿Qué dijo Trump? El presidente estadounidense defendió públicamente al empresario , aunque aclaró que no había hablado con él sobre las acusaciones. “Creo que es un tipo honorable” , dijo Trump a periodistas el domingo. También elogió su trayectoria al frente de Nvidia y sostuvo que había “hecho un trabajo increíble para nuestro país” . “No he hablado con él sobre eso. Solo sé que es una buena persona, pero nunca se sabe lo que está pasando . Espero que todo esté bien”, agregó. President Trump responds to the report that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and he's not rushing to judgment. ⠀ "I think he's an honorable guy," Trump tells reporters, saying he hasn't spoken to Huang about the matter and wants to hear his… pic.twitter.com/p3xV41ydpv — Fox News (@FoxNews) November 8, 2026 Consultado sobre la posibilidad de que Huang lo acompañara en su próximo viaje a Asia, Trump respondió que no lo sabía, pero que “sin duda” lo llevaría . También consideró que el ejecutivo probablemente tendría una explicación sobre lo sucedido y que habría que escucharla. ¿Qué hará Nvidia? La compañía anunció que un comité integrado por directores independientes , con asistencia de asesores externos, supervisará una investigación para determinar si Huang fue objetivo de una operación de inteligencia extranjera y si existió algún riesgo para los secretos comerciales o la seguridad nacional estadounidense. Nvidia aseguró que, hasta el momento, su junta directiva no tiene motivos para creer que se haya comprometido información confidencial de la empresa o que la seguridad nacional de Estados Unidos haya resultado afectada. Huang manifestó su respaldo a la revisión y prometió cooperar plenamente. “Estoy comprometido con la protección de Nvidia y con el apoyo a la seguridad nacional de Estados Unidos” , escribió en su carta a los empleados.

noticias.titulo: Interdisciplinarity on the curriculum—teachers hold different views on what students should learn
noticias.resumen: The climate transition, energy supply and technological development are just some examples of areas where knowledge from several disciplines needs to come together to find relevant solutions. Engineering students are therefore often given the opportunity to work on interdisciplinary projects. But the term "interdisciplinary" encompasses widely differing ideas about what the teaching should involve and what students are actually expected to learn. This is shown by a study in which researchers interviewed 18 teachers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, Aalto University in Finland…
noticias.contenido: The climate transition, energy supply and technological development are just some examples of areas where knowledge from several disciplines needs to come together to find relevant solutions. Engineering students are therefore often given the opportunity to work on interdisciplinary projects. But the term "interdisciplinary" encompasses widely differing ideas about what the teaching should involve and what students are actually expected to learn. This is shown by a study in which researchers interviewed 18 teachers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, Aalto University in Finland and Aalborg University in Denmark. The paper is published in the Journal of Engineering Education.

noticias.titulo: Chirality of 'trions' illuminates new paths for quantum optics
noticias.resumen: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. While electron-hole pairs, or "excitons," were known to keep the chirality of the underlying nanotube, the team showed that adding a charge to create "trions" does not change this property.
noticias.contenido: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. noticias.titulo: SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says
noticias.resumen: "Grok analyzing the same video is 99.9 percent perfect."
noticias.contenido: For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week's UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company's changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world's preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," Dontchev said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars." Read full article Comments

noticias.titulo: Melanie C: From Sporty Spice to dance DJ with 'Sweat'
noticias.resumen: Melanie Chisholm rose to fame in the 1990s with one of the world's biggest girl bands: the Spice Girls. "Melanie C", "Mel C" and "Sporty Spice" were her nicknames. She went on to have a successful solo career with several hits in the 2000s, including "Never Be The Same Again" with the late Lisa Left Eye from TLC. In recent years, she's taken up DJing electronic dance music and recently released her ninth studio album "Sweat". Marjorie Hache caught up with the fitter-than-ever ex-Spice Girl.

noticias.titulo: "Un lienzo en blanco": se vende una isla entera entre Galicia y Portugal en medio de quejas que tildan de disparate construir ahí

noticias.contenido: “Belleza, tranquilidad y libertad de desarrollo”. Así se promociona la venta de Boega, una isla que se abre entre Tomiño y Vila Nova de Cerveira, donde el río Miño raja su cauce como quien extiende los brazos. Este islote de un bosque de verde eléctrico, silencio y pureza no tiene dueño. Por eso ahora, y como documentaban desde La Voz de Galicia , la mayor isla del Miño se ofrece al mejor postor por seis millones de euros. Sale a unos 146.000 euros por hectárea, según mis cuentas. Qué se vende. Según Galiciaé , son unas 41 hectáreas de terreno plano y arbolado, de 1,4 kilómetros de largo y 400 metros de ancho , sin edificios ni infraestructuras. No hay nada, así que puede haber de casi todo. Los anuncios, publicados en Private Islands Online, JamesEdition y Vladi Private Islands, hablan de un “lienzo en blanco”. Entre los usos que sugieren figuran una residencia de lujo, cabañas ecológicas autosuficientes o un santuario natural privado. Solo se llega por barco o helicóptero, y Vladi precisa que está a 45 minutos del aeropuerto de Oporto y a 40 del de Vigo . ¿Isla gallega? Aunque se divise desde Tomiño, A Boega es portuguesa: pertenece a Vila Nova de Cerveira, y su titularidad particular fue delimitada y reconocida en 1952 . Una leyenda local, recogida por el ayuntamiento portugués, atribuye su nombre a un anciano llamado Ega y a su nieto, que lo llamaba Bô. Hoy la propiedad está ligada a una sociedad cuyo capital adquirió íntegramente el fondo BlueCrow Growth Fund I en noviembre de 2021 . En Xataka Alguien vende una isla con castillo en medio de un embalse de Ávila: 11 baños, autosuficiente y 3 millones de euros Sueños sin construir. Hace años se planteó convertirla en campo de golf o en complejo hotelero, y en 2023 llegó el proyecto más ambicioso, Porto Boega, un parque de atracciones presentado en Orlando por la británica Storyland Studios (y ojo que contaba hasta con el respaldo de BlueCrow, uno de los mayores capitales de Portugal). Sin embargo, no se construyó nada; más bien se criticó su posible impacto ambiental sobre un tramo delicado del río. Ser dueño, pero a medias. El anuncio presume de “total flexibilidad arquitectónica”, pero, como recuerda Galiciaé, levantar una vivienda, un hotel o un helipuerto exigiría autorizaciones urbanísticas, ambientales y, en el último caso, aeronáuticas que no vienen con la escritura. En 2023, el fondo presentó un Pedido de Informação Prévia (PIP), el trámite portugués para comprobar si un proyecto es viable, orientado a un uso agrícola. En julio de 2025, los citados BlueCrow lo daban por pendiente, y un anuncio posterior de Vladi asegura que hay un PIP favorable para actividades agrícolas. Es decir, se pueden montar granjas y zonas de cultivo, pero nada de parques temáticos. En Xataka Un hombre se compró una isla desierta en 1962: plantó 16.000 árboles y la convirtió en un santuario anti-ricos El rechazo en la orilla gallega. Tal y como han publicado desde COPE , la puesta a la venta ha provocado un fuerte rechazo entre alcaldes como los de Tui y Tomiño y entre los pescadores del río, aunque la crónica no detalla sus argumentos. El más explícito es el alcalde de Tui, Enrique Cabaleiro, que pide que el Estado portugués o el español la conviertan en propiedad pública. Tiene razón de ser: las administraciones se enfrentan a requisitos ambientales muy estrictos incluso para autorizar una prueba deportiva, y ahora se plantearía dejar a un ente privado emprender una obra de un impacto enorme. Recuerda además que todo el espacio del río pertenece a la Red Natura, el sistema europeo de áreas protegidas, y concluye que “es un disparate hacer ahí un resort o cualquier otra actividad”. Mercado de islas. No es una rareza gallega, aunque sí minoritaria. Ya hay islas privadas como Toralla, la Illa da Creba, las Sisargas u O Santo , este último, un islote de Marín, anunciado en su día por 300.000 euros. En cualquier caso, no consta ningún comprador y el precio es un redondeo que puede bajar o subir según avance el tiempo de la oferta. Quedan sin aclarar el estado real del PIP y la posición de la Câmara de Vila Nova de Cerveira y de la sociedad propietaria, que no figuran en lo publicado. Mientras tanto, la isla no se va a mover de sitio, acaso ganará o perderá unos metros según el caudal del Miño. Imágenes | Tripadvisor En Xataka | Si tienes 400.000 euros al fin puedes cumplir el sueño de poseer tu propia isla. El problema es cómo llegar hasta ella - La noticia "Un lienzo en blanco": se vende una isla entera entre Galicia y Portugal en medio de quejas que tildan de disparate construir ahí fue publicada originalmente en Xataka por Isra Fdez .

noticias.titulo: Hold up — I had a great time talking to the RIAA guy
noticias.resumen: Today, I’m talking with Mitch Glazier, who is CEO and chairman of the RIAA. This conversation was a real full-circle moment for me: I was in college when Napster hit, and the RIAA became everyone’s villain for suing kids for downloading music. noticias.contenido: Today, I’m talking with Mitch Glazier, who is CEO and chairman of the RIAA. This conversation was a real full-circle moment for me: I was in college when Napster hit, and the RIAA became everyone’s villain for suing kids for downloading music. That was when I decided to go be a copyright lawyer, which set the rest of my career in motion — and Mitch was in the background as a young lawyer at the RIAA working on those cases. So part of me was very deeply, very genuinely surprised to discover just how much fun I had talking to Mitch. That’s because here in 2026, Mitch, the RIAA, the record labels, the artists, and ordinary people are all pretty unhappy with the big AI companies in the same way, for training on everyone’s work without permission and flooding our feeds with slop. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Everyone is mad about it! And since the RIAA is both the group that lobbies for changes to the law and also the group that files lawsuits about things that affect record labels and distributors, Mitch is a pretty busy guy these days. We got deep into the legal complexity of things like AI deepfakes, how banning them might affect other kinds of expression, and how the AI detection and labeling systems that we all seem to want might actually work in practice — especially if big platforms like Spotify and YouTube don’t get on board. I just want to get right into it. This conversation is a real ride through how AI, the law, art, and commerce might all intersect. I think you’re going to be able to tell, Mitch and I had a lot of fun talking about it. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube , where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: RIAA CEO Mitch Glazier. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Mitch Glazier, you’re the chairman and CEO of the Recording Industry Association of America, which people know as the RIAA. Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. Thank you, Nilay. I’m excited to be here. I am very excited to talk to you. I have to tell you, this is a very full-circle moment for me. My entire career got on track when I was in college. Napster came out, my university banned Napster from the school network, and I decided right then I was going to go be a copyright lawyer. And then I was a copyright lawyer, and I defended kids who got sued for using Kazaa . I was not good at that job. It was not fulfilling. And I became a journalist because I could write about copyright law on the iPod. So talking to you is about as full circle as it gets for me. Thank you for being on the show. Good. Well then, I’m no longer sorry for the policies that we forced your school to implement because it made you a copyright lawyer. So the world benefited at the end of the day. It had some silver linings to it. When I first started at the RIAA, Napster was obviously the big issue. Nobody had seen anything like it before. The last technological change had really been CDs. I mean, it had been a long time, a much more gradual change and much less abrupt. So they decided it’d be a good idea, since I was youngish at the time, to make me go to college campuses, go to auditoriums, and convince these college students that they shouldn’t use peer-to-peer technology. Wait, wait, wait. I imagine when you said that, it was more like a 21 Jump Street situation, where you were posing in the dining hall being like, “We should pay for it.” Were you giving presentations? Yes, it was horrible. Everybody had these anti-RIAA t-shirts on. I remember one time I followed Chuck D, who was there promoting peer-to-peer. And I didn’t know what to do, and I knew I was going to get booed. So I took a garbage bag, put it over my head, and I walked out onto the stage, thinking they were going to throw tomatoes at me; I might as well make light of it. But I have to say, even though it was a very tough time, some of the conversations that we had with students at that time were some of the best conversations I’ve ever had — even now with AI — about the change in technologies, things being fan-driven, and the disconnect that can occur sometimes between an industry and the people who are out there driving change in the industry. So it was actually a good experience in the end, but it certainly did not feel like it at the time. It didn’t feel like it at the time for me. Thank you for saying the butterfly effect is real. But it was heated. It was hot. One of the things that has really occurred to me as I get older, and AI exists, and I see the platforms taking so much of the economic value out of art, is that my opinions about intellectual property enforcement have changed. It feels like I’m just giving up all of the ideals that I had when I was a kid about the internet, that open access to information was good, that… There was that meme ages ago: everything is a remix, and we should all build on each other’s art as much as we want because that will push the culture forward. I am still very idealistic about that. And I definitely did not think the recording industry suing kids was the appropriate way to protect the intellectual property of artists back then. But here we are in the age of AI, and it feels like no one is making enough money for making art except the world’s biggest artists — who are all also tech investors now in some way — and the tech platforms that collect fractions of pennies from everything and are doing data center build-outs or whatever it is. And that just existential dynamic for me is where I wanted to start. I want to talk about how the RIAA works and all the Decoder questions, but I was just thinking about what I really wanted to ask you, and it comes down to this: we have to protect the work, but there’s some balance in overprotecting the work that makes it harder for people to make new things. And my own journey with the RIAA is a reconsideration of that as more and more things get taken. Where have you landed? You’ve been there for more than 20 years. How are you feeling about that balance? Yeah, so the word balance is the right one, and it’s not an easy one. It’s one of those things where, over time, a barrier pops up here and then you kind of pivot, and then a barrier pops up here and you kind of pivot, and you sort of land in a zone that feels right because the responses that you’re getting, both from the creative community and from fans, start to line up. And I think in AI, they are lining up much more closely than they did during previous years of disruption. Some of it has been because of the democratization of the industry, where the gatekeeping roles have changed, where the partnerships between those who partner and invest with artists and the artists themselves have changed. In a world where artists and label services, like à la carte services, are a bigger part of revenue, in an area where catalog, forever exploitation, and new investors in the industry have come in, the landscape is much wider now. And it’s not like there are just two types of big actors controlling or sharing in all of the money. Now there are dozens of different types of folks meeting artists in different places where they are and meeting fans in different places where they are. And so it feels to me like this disruption, which is huge, and I hope we talk about it… The good news is, unlike Napster, I don’t feel like we are facing it at odds, which is kind of what it felt like back then. Now it feels like we’re not in the same place, but we’re kind of rowing in the same general direction, which is that everybody understands that art and commerce have always had tension, and there’s always going to have to be a balance. But authenticity and that connection between a human being artist and a fan, the preservation of that seems to be paramount in everything that we’re doing, whether you’re investing, listening, or performing. And to me, we’re not fighting in this space anymore between just a business model or an investment. We are now fighting to keep the art as human and the connection between an artist and a fan preserved and alive. And that to me just seems like a much larger purpose, I guess. So it feels very different to me. It feels like a good bookend. Like you, I started my career with Napster, but I was on the other side, learned a ton as a young lawyer, and now on the other side, we have AI, and comparing the two is so wild. I mean, the polls during Napster were like fans over here, and creators kind of hiding a little bit, and the companies over here. And now it’s like AI’s over here, and we’re all together on the other side. Yeah. I mean, again, I cannot emphasize this enough: I was a bad lawyer, and I should not have been doing that job. [Laughs] I doubt that. I was not good at it. I really wasn’t. And what I remember from that time was that it was college kids; their universities would turn over their IP addresses, and they would get their little lawsuit. We would tell them, “We’re going to go to the district court in Chicago; you’re going to settle for $5,000, because that’s what the RIAA is running this program at. It’s a $5,000 settlement to break even on the cost and to deter you, and then you’re going to go work at the pizza place for a semester, pay your bill, and move on.” And I thought, this can’t be accomplishing a goal. The thing I’m doing right now is nothing. And maybe that’s why I felt like I was a horrible lawyer. Maybe that’s why I got out of it. But what you’re describing is the poles there, where there was no pushback on, well, these kids just love music. The thing they love is just music, and now they can get it, and they have it. They weren’t thinking about the business model of CDs. That’s what Napster fundamentally disrupted. There was a scarce physical object that you could go pay $15 for, and if Metallica sold enough of those, their plane would get bigger, and everyone could kind of see that. And, “I’m listening to a lot of this music, and it should make you rich,” was nowhere close to reality. We’ve built those models now. We have built Spotify and Apple Music and all the subscription models. I want to talk about YouTube quite a bit, actually, where you can listen to a lot of music and some people will get rich, but a middle class of artists may just be totally hollowed out. And now the AI companies are like, “And we’re going to set up a competitor where you can just ask for music and no one except us will get paid.” And that is probably built on a bunch of artists that used to make money by having a lot of attention. That swirl for me is the one that I can’t decide where my ideals fit into. As a person who has opened Suno and had a good time just making some music, I’m like, well, I understand how this is great for one kind of person with an artistic bent. I understand why this is fun, as somebody who likes music. I do not understand the economics that follow from this, the same way I had no idea how the economics of disrupting the CD would shake out. I’ll actually give you one example just to make this question even longer. We had the CEO of Cloudflare on the show , and they’re trying to set up a system where, instead of websites running advertising on traffic, everyone gets paid a fraction of a cent to make content on the web, like Spotify. I was like, “Dude, Spotify changed the entire music industry. Artists have different jobs now because of that economic model.” And he was like, “No, I think the big ones are really happy.” And you can argue with him or not argue with him, but it felt to me like the tech industry did not understand what that disruption actually did to music at that moment. Now we’re standing on the precipice of it again. So again, I just want to start there. I’m feeling this existential tension; you described it as art and commerce, where commerce is going to change, and so art has to change as well. How are you thinking about that? Since we’re talking about existential things, if you go back to why copyright exists, it’s to create more opportunities for more art in the future. That’s why copyright exists. That’s the reason why the property right exists. It’s to create an incentive to allow people to protect their creations so that they will go ahead and make a living doing it. We don’t want this just to be a hobby. We want this to be… Artists are extraordinary people in our culture. They are geniuses who need to be incentivized to share that genius because they’re not normal people. They’re not me. These are incredible people who have something to share, and if they can’t make a living doing it, then they can’t and won’t share it, and we are all worse off. That’s the whole purpose of copyright, is to be able to allow them to be able to benefit from that in some way, shape, or form. Now, obviously all this infrastructure has grown up around it, all these companies have grown up around it, et cetera, but that’s sort of the basic premise. And you have to ask yourself the question: if non-human music, which can be made in two seconds without lived experience and, in my view, without a soul, can dilute or drown out the incentives for people to be able to make a living as humans making art, what happens? What happens to our culture? And I think that is an existential question that is not just academic to ask. We could talk about differentiation in the marketplace; we can talk about whether or not Taylor Swift competing with an indie grunge band is the right model for everybody to be able to get their piece of the business on these streaming services. But at its core, it’s still essentially human, and it still distributes art that took sometimes 20 years to make, sometimes three minutes to make. It depends on the genius of the artist doing it, but it still has all of those human warts and craft. It has craft. I think that if you have a system where the incentive is with the tech company that makes the AI to use everything that humanity has ever created to make money and, at the same time, then deplete the opportunity for future human music, we’re going to have a society that is one way going backwards and another way going forwards. If the culture suffers going forwards more than improving on what went backwards, we are in the wrong place, and we’re not doing the right things. And that’s what I mean about sort of rowing together. I live in the policy world. You have to ask yourself, what policies can we put in place to create the incentives to allow that better future of human-made music? It’s really hard. It’s super hard. When I say I’m having this existential dilemma… Just to put it into clear focus for the listener: In the age of the CD, the economic value was tied to a scarce physical object. There are only so many CDs. And then you could maybe copy CDs, and Apple would get in trouble for saying that you could rip, mix, and burn CDs. That was a whole ad campaign, and Apple got in trouble for incentivizing people to copy CDs. But you would pay money for an object that existed, and then we got to the digital world, and the friction to copy the song went to zero. We had to invent a new model, and that model looks like Spotify and the rest. Now we’re in the age of AI, and the friction to create might be going to zero. So there’s even less scarcity because you can just horsepower an AI pop star into existence singing an AI song, and there’s going to be a glut of supply. Somewhere in there is marketing, somewhere in there is fandom. There’s all this stuff that can create other kinds of scarcity, but that’s the journey the music industry has been on. I always say whatever happens to the music industry happens to everybody else five years later. The music industry is always on the cutting edge. Where does the new scarcity come from in this model? Is it you doing policy work and lobbying governments for changes to the laws? Is it fans revolting and saying, “We want human artists”? Is it the platforms labeling everything? Where does the scarcity come back in? You’re the first person, I think, that I’ve listened to who has honed in on this particular question. At the end of the day, it’s always the fans, in my view. They will always win, because if you are any kind of service, with any kind of business model — I don’t care if you’re AI, I don’t care if you’re streaming — you need human beings to pay you money, usually by subscribing, as that’s the highest revenue source. And they’re not going to do that if they feel like they are losing out. I do think, given all of the focus groups, polling, everything that we’ve done, and other people have done on this, it is very clear that fans want to maintain a human connection with an artist. It’s not just about the music. It’s also about the artist, the persona, the brand, the emotional connection. Taylor Swift’s fans love her music, but they also love her. Pearl Jam’s fans love their music, but it’s also, like, Pearl Jam. You know what I mean? They’re their own piece of culture. And so we know, for example, that if a fan knows that a song is AI, then they have a different view of it than if they know that it is human. Do you think that’s going to last forever? I’m honestly curious about this. It has changed even in the last year. It has. I think that, with generative AI, it will last forever. That’s the thing that they’re doing; they’re a pure-play business in that way, and they have a lot of incentives for AI music to replace the music they have to otherwise pay for on that platform. They have a lot of incentives for white noise and fake streams in history to do these things, and they’ve gotten in trouble for some of it. This is a real thing that happens on this platform. Are they going to participate in a labeling scheme and say, “This is AI music?” I think so, because as much as they have an economic incentive to lower their costs, their biggest economic incentive is to keep fans paying $9.99, $12.99, $15.99 per month. And so if fans feel duped, if you are putting — Is that proven out in the market? I’m actually very curious about this. Yes. You’re saying there’s AI slop on Spotify now, or when you search for Taylor Swift, you get a bunch of weird Taylor Swift soundalikes, which is an experience everyone has on Spotify. It hasn’t churned those fans yet. There’s not some exodus to Tidal or Apple Music. Spotify is still dominant in its way. Right. I think they’re walking down the road slowly, probably a little too slowly. I’m trying to see if they can do just enough to keep those two things in balance. Right now, for example, Spotify is saying, “We will only disclose or label a recording as AI in the credits.” Well, how many people look at the credits? I wish more people looked at the credits; they would discover producers and songwriters and other awesome folks who have contributed to the recording — but they don’t. They need to do it at the track level. They’re not there yet. But they are disclosing AI personas that are made, because that’s sort of the highest on the dupe scale. And then under that, they’re looking at the fact that 90 percent of the recordings available on Spotify get 10 percent of the revenue, and 10 percent of the content gets 90 percent of the revenue. It’s because most of what’s on there gets less than 10 listens, or less than a hundred listens, and all of this slop is just going on, which means storage costs and all sorts of other things that they have to think about. So I think that they will go as far down the road as fans will demand, as their users will demand. I think we’ll get to a point where people get these recommendations in their algorithm. “If you like this song, you’ll also like this one.” And when you listen to it, it turns out it was AI, you didn’t know it was AI, and you’ll feel deceived. That’s when they’ve got a giant problem because they’re responsible for that recommendation. They’re the ones that fed that to you. And we do have lots of consumer research out there showing that subscribers, just like all consumers, want to feel like nobody’s pulling the wool over their eyes. But is there an actual market pressure? I can think of all kinds of times fans have revolted against Spotify. I love the band Stars, and every now and again they’ll tweet, “We didn’t make any money on this song on Spotify.” And everyone tweets at Spotify, and they’re mad. Spotify’s not paying artists any more money. Is there an actual market pressure that will make this labeling happen, or is it policy pressure? It’s both. It’s a combination, because there are already laws in other countries that are mandating labels. And once a market like the EU or the US — that’s such a big market — or the UK or China, once they demand labeling on a global system, it’s actually cheaper to do it all around the world than it is to just geo-block it in one country. This is the California car emission model of regulation, right? It’s amazing what California can do because these companies are headquartered there. I mean not Spotify, but Apple and Google and others. And so the transparency law in California is the reason why Suno has to, as of August, put a watermark saying, “This is AI-generated” that’s machine-readable. One state, but they’re doing it all over the world because that’s what… So it’s a combination of policy, which obviously we are very directly engaged in, and competition. I predict that what Apple decides to do that is more fan-friendly will drive Spotify, and vice versa. There’s not that much churn between them, but if there’s some sort of perception that you’re being more subscriber-friendly than somebody else, that tends to drive results. It does the same on the privacy issue, for example, where there’s no law on it, but now companies are competing to say, “We’re the private browser. Apple, we protect your privacy.” One company says that. Let me ask you this. I’ve only got a few minutes left, and I want to take one turn at the end to talk about how you measure for platinum certification, because that’s also up in the air. But let me just ask you one more question here on labeling. We have spent a lot of time at The Verge covering labels for images and media. There are all these standards that exist. I have one poor reporter, her name is Jess Weatherbed, and she has been forced to learn everything about the C2PA standard and content, SynthID, and all these things. I’m so sorry. It’s really important, though. They’re very important, and we spend a lot of time covering them because they have to work. And they have to work in a number of different places in the chain, right? They have to work in the camera, in Photoshop, on Twitter, and everyone has to agree. If Elon Musk does not want SynthID to show up on his platform, it doesn’t matter if it worked in the camera. This is a big chain. It seems harder in music, much harder because a bunch of bedroom DJs are probably not going to participate in your technical scheme for labeling when they upload to DistroKid. An artist getting a beat from a producer over iMessage — who knows if that metadata will survive. You might have to watermark the sound files themselves in some deep intrinsic way, and that can get you into all kinds of trouble because now you’re screwing with the audio files at the software level and artists don’t like that. How do you make labeling work at all? Yeah, you’re hitting on our daily meetings. So I mean, there are the international organizations like DDEX, for example, that can help align fields and stuff like that. C2PA, which can give you a model for provenance. But at the end of the day, it has to be the platforms and the distributors that are willing to do it. Because when it comes to generative AI, the record labels are not tagging and putting generative AI up on Spotify. That’s out of the DIY world. That’s somebody going to a music generator, downloading it, and putting it up through DistroKid. So your gateway is DistroKid, TuneCore. It’s the distributors. Are they using AI detection technology to determine that it’s fully generated? You might not be able to use AI detection technology to say your song is five percent of this or use it for attribution yet, but you can definitely use it to say this is fully generated AI. And if so, are they willing to tag it so that it works with Apple and Spotify’s platform? Then, on the platforms themselves, this is sort of like the parental advisory program; it might be voluntary, and everybody might have a little bit of a different way of implementing it, but fans are pretty clear. When something’s labeled as parental advisory, which probably just draws more young people to listen to it — It did to me. But when it’s labeled as parental advisory, people kind of get it. They know. It’s become sort of a culturally known thing. I think labeling for fully generated AI can definitely get there, but the distributors have to be willing to play. It can’t just be the platforms because if it doesn’t go downstream, they’re going to go in different directions. And already, Deezer’s going in one direction, Apple’s going in another direction, Spotify’s going in another direction. To me, the fully generated problem, which is a DIY problem, is a distributor problem. And we have to provide incentives to the distributors to get them to take responsibility and play ball. Do you think that technology exists to support the policy there? You need a technology that can detect AI-generated media. I’m not sure that any of that exists or works well. I think it exists and works well for fully generated AI music. We also do a lot of testing at the RIAA. That’s another thing that our tech team does. And then we disclose the results back to the folks who gave it to us. We won’t disclose it to anybody else, but if you want to know what our test says about your technology, we’ll tell you. And I think when it comes to fully generated AI, there’s plenty of detection technologies out there that do a really good job. Once you get below that, time will make it better. So I don’t know that we could get into a lot of gradations right now. Deezer, very successfully, on a platform level, uses AI detection technology and then labels what it detects as fully generated AI, and it’s got a very low false positive rate. I want to end by talking about the certifications for platinum records and so on. It’s an important part of what you do. All the artists want their little records on their wall. It’s amazing that it’s still records. One of our jokes at The Verge is also that no one knows how to count anything, that Nielsen ratings — I should probably disclose, we are now part of the company that owns Luminate, which powers the Billboard charts. The Billboard charts and their methodology are always in flux. Actually, I think as of this year, they’re in a fight with YouTube. YouTube does not want to be counted on the Billboard charts because some methodologies are… Counting is very political. It is. You literally give awards for counting to a big number. That is in flux as artists gain more attention on TikTok. And I have probably heard that whole Nicole Kidman song, in fragments on TikTok. I’ve never listened to the whole thing all the way through, and I’m certainly never going to buy a copy of it. Again, all in flux, and then somewhere in there is a bunch of AI remixes, and now I’ve listened to “Pop Star” by Drake 10,000 times because Darth Vader is singing it to me. How are you thinking about that methodology, as to who’s creating what? AI is in the mix, and we’re listening to more and more fragments to discover songs on social platforms than anything else. I swear to God, you are in my daily meetings. Can I just tell you? I’m happy to hear that. I drive The Verge team crazy because I’m like, the music industry is the future always. And they’re like, no one wants to listen to that. So thank you for indulging me. I appreciate you. I mean, you have your finger on the pulse. This is exactly the type of stuff we’re thinking of. So right now we’re still in the world of 1500 streams equaling one unit, and what used to be the sale of a CD. Now it’s obviously singles-based more than albums-based, although we still do certify albums. And if you look at the chart eligibility program that is now being implemented outside of Billboard and OCC, in other places of the world, they have made rules to say, unless it’s substantially human , we are not going to allow it to be eligible for the chart because you’re literally taking the place of a human artist on number 49. Billboard, so far, will allow it, but they’ll label it. We haven’t, because we certify albums that were released by record companies. We have yet to run into the issue of the AI slop or the machine-created piece. But as we get more into assistive AI, as creators start to use AI more, and you look at the chart eligibility of substantially human, does a stream as part of that 1500 mean that it still has to be a human stream? Yes, I’m sure that we will come down on that side. But what does substantially human mean? I think over time that might change. It might be different three years from now than it is today. But at the core, it’s got to be in the control of the creator. And some people would argue that putting nine words into a music generator is an act of creation. Oh, they will. They’re going to. Yeah. And that they are a creator, and therefore it’s the same thing. It’s not the same thing. Not saying that craft doesn’t change over time, and that in songwriting it’s also different than in producing and creating a recording. Using AI in the songwriting process may look very different than it does in the recording process, so we have to think about that too. But as far as gold and platinum go, we are still in the reliably safe zone of being able to know with a great deal of certainty exactly what we’re doing. I think the evolution over time is going to be in how creators use AI more than it will need to be in something that’s fully machine-readable or machine-created. Well, Mitch, you’ve given us so much time. As you can tell, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed this conversation. I could keep going for hours and hours now. Me too. I mean, honestly, this has been awesome. You freaked me out a little bit because you… It’s so great to see, though, because the stuff that you’re focused on is exactly what we are trying to grapple with every single day. And I think where we’ve come to is that we can’t pretend that there are easy answers. We can’t just react sort of in a knee-jerk way. We’ve got to try to figure out a path forward that’s going to allow the industry to change and grow. This industry’s adapted more times than any other industry in the history of our country. I mean, nobody goes from wax cylinders to AI in a hundred years. Can you imagine asking Boeing to make cars? So, a very adaptable industry. I agree with you that we’re ahead of the game and that we are the future. We’re sort of living it. And the lessons that we learned from the music industry, we can apply to a lot of other things. So this has been awesome. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Really appreciate it. You got it. Take care.

noticias.titulo: How bacteria build the molecular bushing of the flagellar motor
noticias.resumen: The bacterial flagellum is a motility organelle that enables bacteria to swim and is composed of more than 30 different proteins. Researchers have long sought to understand how this complex nanomachine self-assembles from many parts in the correct order and at the correct positions. In a study published in Communications Biology, a research team at the University of Osaka revealed the mechanism by which the flagellar motor assembles its bushing around the drive shaft.
